ClinicalDocument.title: SYNTHETIC RECORD, NOT A REAL MEDICAL RECORD — Gastroenterology Consultation — Marcus Aurelius

code.originalText: Gastroenterology consultation with upper endoscopy and biopsy, review of the CT coronary angiogram, diagnosis of erosive esophagitis, and start of omeprazole

text.paragraph: Chronic burning and pressing pain in the upper abdomen and lower chest after meals for more than a year, with poor appetite, night waking and a 3 kg weight loss, in a 53-year-old man who takes an opium-containing herbal remedy. ECG normal; CT coronary angiography booked for the morning of your appointment. Please perform upper endoscopy with gastric biopsies, find the cause, and advise on treatment. [S]

Urgency: Routine but prompt, within one week. He is stable, with no bleeding, difficulty swallowing or vomiting. No acid-suppressing drug has been started before the endoscopy; he has calcium carbonate as needed. He has been told to call 911 for chest pain at rest lasting more than a few minutes, or with breathlessness, sweating or fainting. [S]

list.item: Is there an esophageal, gastric or duodenal cause for his pain after meals: reflux esophagitis, peptic ulcer, or functional dyspepsia?
Does he have Helicobacter pylori infection?
What treatment do you advise, and for how long?
Could the opium in his remedy be contributing, through slowed stomach emptying or esophageal dysmotility, and does he need manometry or emptying studies?
Does he need repeat endoscopy or other follow-up?

text.paragraph: Mr. Aurelius, a 53-year-old man who leads a large organization on a long field assignment, is seen at the request of Dr. Ashworth-Nnamdi one week after his first visit. For more than a year he has had burning and pressure behind the lower breastbone and in the upper abdomen about half an hour after eating, worst after the single large meal he eats late at night shortly before lying down, with a sour taste in the mouth and waking at night. Antacid eases it within minutes. It does not come on with exertion. He has no difficulty or pain swallowing, vomiting, black stools or blood. His appetite has been poor and he has lost about 3 kg. He takes no NSAIDs, has never smoked, and drinks wine two or three times a week. He has taken an opium-containing herbal paste at bedtime most nights for about six years; he spoke about it openly and asked that it not be judged. Hard stools every two or three days. He had CT coronary angiography this morning. [S]
Historical basis. These claims are historical evidence, not findings from a modern examination.

list.item: Marcus Aurelius was born at Rome, in a villa on the Caelian Hill, on the sixth day before the Kalends of May (26 April in the Julian calendar) in 121 CE. [D]
He was educated in rhetoric by Fronto, was adopted by the emperor Antoninus Pius in 138 CE, became emperor in 161 CE, at first jointly with Lucius Verus, and ruled alone from 169 CE. [D]

Much of his reign was spent on campaign in central Europe, and the Meditations were probably written there, about 171 to 175 CE; the first book ends 'Among the Quadi at the Granua' and the second 'This in Carnuntum'. [D]

A great pestilence struck the empire during his reign, from 165 CE, spread with the Parthian war and the wars on the Danube; the Life of Marcus says the dead were removed in carts and wagons and that thousands died, many nobles among them. Galen witnessed the epidemic. [D]
The cause of the Antonine Plague is uncertain: Galen's case reports suggest smallpox to many authors, but paleopathological confirmation is lacking. [R]

Cassius Dio, a senator of the period, writes that he was so frail in body that at first he could not endure the cold, that he ate very little and only at night, and that by day he took nothing but the drug called theriac, 'not so much because he feared anything, as because his stomach and chest were in bad condition'. [D]

In the Meditations he thanks the gods that remedies were shown to him in dreams, among them remedies 'against bloodspitting and giddiness', and that his body had held out so long in such a kind of life. [D]

Galen became court physician to the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus, and prepared his theriac at the court; Marcus Aurelius took theriac daily, to protect against poisons and for his general health. [D]
Theriac was a compound remedy of many ingredients, among them viper's flesh, opium, honey, wine and cinnamon. [D]
Galen relates that the emperor disliked the drowsiness the theriac caused, so the poppy juice was left out; he then could not sleep, and the opium-containing preparation was resumed. [D]

Whether he was dependent on or addicted to opium is disputed. Thomas Africa argued for addiction in 1961; later reviews find no explicit ancient description of opium dependence, call his the one putative case, and favour the most parsimonious reading, that the opium was medicinal rather than hedonic. [R]
As a boy he studied so hard that it impaired his health, which the Life of Marcus calls the only fault to be found in his entire childhood. [D]

text.paragraph: No results recorded at this visit.

list.item: Reflux disease with erosive esophagitis, Los Angeles grade B, with a small hiatal hernia (K21.00). This explains his symptoms: burning and pressure after a large meal eaten shortly before lying down, night waking with a sour taste, and relief with antacid, with coronary disease excluded this morning. There is no ulcer, so peptic ulcer disease is excluded, and functional dyspepsia is not the diagnosis when a structural cause is found. Grade B esophagitis heals in most patients with eight weeks of a proton pump inhibitor. [S]
Helicobacter pylori. The rapid urease test is negative off acid suppression and the stomach looks normal; histology will confirm. If it is negative, no eradication therapy is needed. [S]

Opium-containing remedy and the gut (F11.90). Opioids slow stomach emptying and can disturb esophageal motility, and in long-term users can cause an opioid-induced esophageal dysfunction; they also cause his constipation. The esophagitis seen today is a reflux injury and should be treated in its own right. Manometry or a gastric emptying study is not needed now, since the endoscopy explains his symptoms; it would be if symptoms persisted despite healing, or if swallowing became difficult. Any change in the remedy is his decision, and is best planned with Dr. Ashworth-Nnamdi. [S]

text.paragraph: Data reviewed: Dr. Ashworth-Nnamdi's intake note and results: normal ECG; hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; normal liver tests and lipase; urine drug test with morphine and codeine only. CT coronary angiography this morning: coronary calcium score 0, no plaque or stenosis (CAD-RADS 0). Upper endoscopy this morning under moderate sedation: mucosal breaks longer than 5 mm in the distal esophagus, not continuous between folds (Los Angeles grade B); a 2 cm sliding hiatal hernia; no Barrett's mucosa, stricture or ring; normal stomach with no ulcer or erosion; normal duodenum. Biopsies from the antrum, incisura and body for histology and a rapid urease test, which is negative. [S]

list.item: Omeprazole 20 mg 30 to 60 minutes before breakfast for eight weeks, then stop and use it on demand for heartburn; return to daily therapy at the lowest dose if heartburn comes back most days. [S]
Stop the calcium carbonate once omeprazole has started. [S]
The main meal at least three hours before lying down, the head of the bed raised, and little or no wine at night. [S]
Helicobacter pylori: no treatment if the histology is negative, as the rapid urease test suggests. [S]
No repeat endoscopy for grade B esophagitis while he is well; repeat endoscopy for difficulty swallowing, bleeding, weight loss or symptoms that fail to settle. [S]
High-resolution esophageal manometry and reflux monitoring off therapy only if symptoms persist despite eight weeks of treatment. [S]
No change to the remedy is needed for the esophagitis to heal; if he chooses to reduce it, a slow pace planned with his primary clinician, and polyethylene glycol for constipation meanwhile. [S]

Discussed with Dr. Ashworth-Nnamdi the same morning; she continues the prescribing and the follow-up. The endoscopy pictures were shown to Mr. Aurelius, who was relieved to hear that his heart is sound and that the problem can be treated. [S]

Follow-up: No routine gastroenterology follow-up; Dr. Ashworth-Nnamdi will send the histology result, and he will be seen again if symptoms persist after the eight-week course or alarm features appear. [S]
